A TEA was conducted and BAF and ORH were selected the selected airports due to proximity to feedstock and to represent locations in Western Massachusetts and near Boston. The highest biofuel production potential was using select MSW within a 100-mile radii resulting in estimated annual production of 336 million gallons (BAF) and 278 million gallons (ORH). The woody biomass TEA was conducted for PWM with potential production of 53 million gallons per year. It takes several years to build a new biofuels plant. Therefore, for the foreseeable future, SAF produced outside of New England is expected to be delivered pre-blended due to existing production volumes, terminal space constraints, infrastructure availability, and limitations in the ability of some terminals to receive fuel by multiple modes. Deliveries of SAF/Jet A blends results in business as usual for New England jet fuel infrastructure, and the investment to handle SAF would occur upstream of New England. In the longer term, enabling SAF produced in New England requires more consideration and planning due to infrastructure constraints. For example, the terminal with the highest jet fuel volume that serves BOS and other airports is limited in space and can only receive fuels by barge or tanker, not truck. It is recommended that future regional SAF producers should work with terminals identified in this report that can receive fuel by truck and offload by barge or tanker to ensure supply to BOS, the largest consumer of Jet A in New England. Many terminal owners expressed willingness to work with future SAF producers to enable blending and delivery to airports within the region. Future potential work could include a detailed siting analysis to identify ideal sites for production evaluating closed industrial sites, brownfield sites, and similar. Such an analysis could consider market competition to identify the most viable locations for SAF development.
